Not quite sure if this is appropriate in #lean4 or #general but I encounter this sometimes:

import Mathlib

example (s : Finset ℕ) (simProc : s = ∅) : {x ∈ s | True}.attach = ∅ := by
  rw [simProc] -- works
  sorry

example (s : Finset ℕ) (simProc : s = ∅) : {x ∈ s | True}.attach = ∅ := by
  simp_rw [simProc] -- fails
  sorry

If simProc were a real simproc, then the first example wouldn't work either. Does rw fundamentally not support simprocs? If not, are there plans to make simprocs compatible with rw (and erw, etc)?

rw fundamentally does not support simprocs, and to support simprocs would essentially require a completely separate tactic that rw would call.

It's an interesting suggestion though. In a full RFC, I'd imagine there would be a rwproc (rw and simp have different monads and different expectations on what the tactic is doing to an expression), but there could be some metaprogramming adaptors to create one from the other, to share code.
#24155 discusses how to hack in rw_procs today

(continuing my message) I'm currently rewriting rw, so I'll keep the possibility in mind. It seems very useful too, well beyond the suggested use case of being able to do tricky dependent rewrites that are outside the scope of simp. It also is a potential way to let rw do reductions, e.g. rw [reduce], rw [reduce -zeta], etc., by having a reduce procedure.

@Eric Wieser You scared me for a moment with that hack, since to support rewriting under binders, rw lemmas are going to need to be fully elaborated, rather than the current interleaved elaboration strategy. Or at least that's what we should assume to be necessary unless there's some new idea that would allow reliable transportation of partially elaborated expressions into new contexts, and a way to "cancel" elaborations that are no longer needed.

Your hack appears to be OK since by eta_tac is run before rewriting begins. I was assuming the worst, that you were relying on rw finding a match and then running eta_tac later. Thankfully not!

I was assuming the worst, that you were relying on rw finding a match and then running eta_tac later.

I think I had originally hoped this was how it worked, so that I could get away with rw [eta]...
Unfortunately it does work that way, but rw artificially stops you from doing it here because the LHS of the elaborated lemma is a metavariable.
